# Telegram Serverless

> Run backend code for your bot and Mini App directly on Telegram's infrastructure.

Source: https://core.telegram.org/bots/serverless

Snapshot of the supplied Markdown, not a live reference.
Read the relevant section and follow its local links.

- [Complete documentation](llms-full.txt): All sections in one file.

- [Recent changes](sections/recent-changes.md)
- [October 6, 2026](sections/october-6-2026.md): - Added Mini App hosting. The build output of your Mini App's front‑end is deployed together with the bot and served at https://app<app_id>.tgcloud.ai/.

## Why serverless

- [Why serverless](sections/why-serverless.md): A Telegram bot is, at heart, a program that reacts to updates. Traditionally you had to host that program somewhere that is always on, reachable, and secure — and then keep it that

## Projects and modules

- [Projects and modules](sections/projects-and-modules.md): A serverless project is an ordinary folder under version control. Everything the platform runs sits in one folder, tgcloud/; the rest of the project is yours — a mini‑app front‑end
- [Anatomy of a project](sections/anatomy-of-a-project.md): example_bot/
- [The module system](sections/the-module-system.md): At runtime, a module can see exactly two things: the platform SDK and the other modules in your project. There are no npm packages, no filesystem, and no network except through the
- [Handlers](sections/handlers.md): A handler is a module in handlers/ whose default export the platform invokes when a matching update arrives.
- [Endpoints](sections/endpoints.md): An endpoint is a module in endpoints/ that your Mini App calls — the place for anything the front‑end can't do on its own, like reading and writing the database, calling the Bot AP
- [What gets deployed](sections/what-gets-deployed.md): When you npx tgcloud push, the CLI gathers every .js file under schema.js, lib/, handlers/, and endpoints/, and sends that exact set as your project's module space — together with 
- [Mini App front-end](sections/mini-app-front-end.md): The project root is yours, and it is the natural place for your Mini App's front‑end — built with React, Vue, Svelte or plain HTML, by Vite or any other bundler. Serverless hosts i

## The database

- [The database](sections/the-database.md): Every bot gets its own database — an SQLite‑backed store that persists between invocations and is available to every module through db. You describe your tables in schema.js with a
- [Declaring tables](sections/declaring-tables.md): Tables are named exports in schema.js. Calling table() builds a description at load time (it does not touch the database); the platform discovers the exported tables when you deplo
- [No foreign keys](sections/no-foreign-keys.md): The runtime runs with PRAGMA foreign_keys off. A declared foreign key would be silently inert — no cascades, no orphan protection — which is worse than having none at all, so the D
- [Querying](sections/querying.md): db is a fluent query builder. Every query is asynchronous — the terminal methods (.all(), .get(), .values(), .run()) return Promises, so always await.
- [Migrations](sections/migrations.md): Your database changes as your bot grows. The platform keeps that safe by separating deploying code from changing data, and by classifying every schema change by how risky it is.

## The SDK

- [The SDK](sections/the-sdk.md): At runtime a module has one library: sdk. It bundles the three things a bot backend needs — a database, the Telegram Bot API, and outbound HTTP — with nothing to install and no cre
- [The Bot API](sections/the-bot-api.md): api gives you the entire Telegram Bot API. Call any method as api.<method>(params). Every current — and future — Bot API method works with no SDK update required.
- [HTTP](sections/http.md): fetch is a fetch‑like client for calling the outside world — third‑party APIs, webhooks, anything over HTTP.
- [Logging](sections/logging.md): The standard global console is available — nothing to import, it's just there as in any JavaScript. Its output is captured and shown by npx tgcloud run, which makes it your primary

## Command-line interface

- [Command-line interface](sections/command-line-interface.md): tgcloud is the bridge between your project folder and the cloud. It scaffolds projects, shows you what changed, deploys, runs modules, and applies database migrations. It needs Nod
- [Authentication](sections/authentication.md): A project is tied to one bot by its token, which has the form app<id>:<secret>. The app<id> part is public and may be printed; the secret never appears in logs or errors.
- [`init`](sections/init.md): npx tgcloud init
- [`add`](sections/add.md): npx tgcloud add <target
- [`login`](sections/login.md): npx tgcloud login
- [`status`](sections/status.md): npx tgcloud status
- [`diff`](sections/diff.md): npx tgcloud diff
- [`push`](sections/push.md): npx tgcloud push [files...]
- [`migrate`](sections/migrate.md): npx tgcloud migrate
- [`run`](sections/run.md): npx tgcloud run <module> [args] [--ctx <json5>]
- [`fetch`](sections/fetch.md): npx tgcloud fetch
- [`pull`](sections/pull.md): npx tgcloud pull
- [`reset`](sections/reset.md): npx tgcloud reset
- [`webhook`](sections/webhook.md): npx tgcloud webhook
- [`completion`](sections/completion.md): Note: tab‑completion works only when a bare tgcloud is on your PATH — so install it globally (npm install -g @tgcloud/cli) or otherwise put the binary on your PATH. It can't hook i
- [`upgrade`](sections/upgrade.md): npx tgcloud upgrade [--dry-run]
- [Staying in sync](sections/staying-in-sync.md): Every project has a monotonically increasing revision in the cloud, bumped on each deploy. The CLI remembers the revision it last synced with and sends it on each push. If the clou
